summary:
Visitors in Sokoto State stand under two overlapping penal regimes. Nationally, Nigeria's Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 criminalises same-sex conduct for everyone including tourists, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment; Human Rights Watch (October 2016) records that it also bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, public shows of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, and that police have invoked it to justify torture and arbitrary arrests. The UK Home Office country policy note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) records same-sex sex between men as criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and Sharia law in all twelve northern states criminalising same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions.

Sokoto State's own religious penal code took effect on 31 January 2001. Male same-sex activity is punished by stoning to death where the offender is or has been married, and by 100 lashes otherwise; sexual acts between women draw ta'azir punishment of up to 100 lashes and/or imprisonment. Sokoto is listed among the twelve states whose Shari'a criminal codes apply to Muslims, with maximum penalties of death for men and whipping and/or imprisonment for women for same-sex acts.

The code is not a dead letter. On 9 October 2001 the Upper Sharia Court at Gwadabawa in Sokoto State convicted Safiyatu Hussaini Tungar Tudu of zina under sections 128-129 of the Sokoto State Sharia Penal Code and sentenced her to death by stoning, discharging and acquitting the co-accused. She appealed on 26 October 2001 and the Sharia Court of Appeal of Sokoto State quashed the conviction and discharged and acquitted her on 25 March 2002. The sentence concerned zina rather than same-sex conduct, but it establishes that Sokoto's religious courts apply the state Sharia Penal Code in practice, including the capital-punishment framework the code carries for married men's same-sex acts.

The legislative groundwork is documented at state level: an interim committee report was submitted to Sokoto Governor Attahiru Dalhatu Bafarawa on 13 October 1999 and a final report with an annexe draft bill to establish Sharia courts followed on 16 December 1999.

Gender expression carries separate exposure. Northern states also criminalise cross-dressing: Kano imposes up to one year for men who dress or behave as women, and a northern Islamic court imposed 10 lashes for cross-dressing. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public; whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here. Trans identity itself is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute.

Violence against trans people is documented nationally. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, a TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in Abuja hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing, and the Dial (February 2025) records that six months after the killing no suspects had been charged. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that Okafor, a 24-year-old man stopped by Lagos police, was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay.

The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice for Nigeria, as reported by Sahara Reporters, warns LGBT+ travellers of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states. Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people.

No Sokoto-specific custody finding is available: there is no documented arrest, trial or custody case in the state, no record of where trans prisoners are housed, no trans special unit, and no solitary or segregation practice.
tangentialFactors:
Sokoto's regime is one data point within a wider northern pattern. Twelve states operate Shari'a criminal codes applying to Muslims, and the cross-dressing prohibition cited for Kano, carrying up to one year, together with the 10 lashes imposed by a northern Islamic court for cross-dressing, indicates that gender-expression offences are being used across the zone rather than confined to a single state.

The Safiyatu Hussaini Tungar Tudu case is the closest documented analogue for how Sokoto's religious courts handle capital charges, but it concerned zina and not same-sex conduct, and the death sentence was overturned on appeal within five months. It therefore evidences procedural operation of the code rather than a settled pattern of execution for sexual offences.

Enforcement against perceived sexuality in Nigeria frequently occurs outside formal adjudication. Police extortion and beatings, app-based luring and blackmail, and the weaponisation of the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act described by those affected point to a climate of hostility that operates independently of any single statute's text.

Placement of trans prisoners between male and female sections appears to be left to official discretion rather than governed by written rule, at least in the one nationally prominent case that reached an investigative panel.
localsOnly:
Residents of Sokoto State, Muslim residents in particular, are subject to the Sokoto State Sharia Penal Code alongside the national Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014, so the exposure is cumulative rather than alternative.

Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman, pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, served in a maximum-security prison in Lagos before release on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to discretion. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.

Transgender Nigerians live under the pressure of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public, reported by Reuters in September 2022, alongside the existing northern cross-dressing provisions such as Kano's one-year penalty.

Nigeria provides no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people, and the 2014 Act reinforced colonial-era criminalisation rather than replacing it.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the proposals to criminalise cross-dressing reported in September 2022 have been enacted into law is unresolved in the sources available here.

No Sokoto-specific arrest, trial or custody case involving a trans person is documented in the inventory, and there is no sourced record of where trans prisoners are held in the state, whether a trans special unit exists, or what solitary or segregation practice applies. These are absences of evidence rather than findings of safety.

The Safiyatu Hussaini Tungar Tudu conviction and sentence concerned zina and not same-sex conduct; the inventory does not establish any actual enforcement of the same-sex provisions of the Sokoto State Sharia Penal Code against an identified person.

The sources do not state whether the Sokoto State Sharia Penal Code applies to non-Muslim visitors or only to Muslims, and do not resolve how the code interacts with the national Act in charging practice.
